newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Internet moguls urge Clinton's help in cyberspace.
newsitem.headline: Internet moguls urge Clinton's help in cyberspace.

text.p: Internet moguls urged Bill Clinton on Wednesday to reconsider Washington's strong support for controversial draft pacts to police copyrights in cyberspace, saying they risked choking the multi-billion-dollar industry.

In a letter addressed to the U.S. president, the chairmen of leading U.S. network providers raised the stakes in the battle for copyright legislation on the information superhighway and threatened to block its ratification by the Congress.

The U.S. administration is a strong supporter of the pacts being negotiated under the auspices of the U.N.'s World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO) in Geneva, while an array of consumer, academic and technical groups oppose them.

The presidents of 11 U.S. service giants including America Online, BellSouth Corporation and CompuServe said the pact gave broad powers to copyright-based industries like entertainment and music and exposed them to multi-billion-dollar liability.
"As CEO's of America's leading Internet, online and communication companies, we write to express our great concern about the draft language," they said in the letter to Clinton.

"We urge you to reconsider the Administraation's current position before the WIPO Convention makes a final determination on the issue," said the letter, distributed at a Geneva briefing by members of the Ad Hoc Copyright Coalition, a broad grouping of online service providers including At&T and Netscape.
The Internet, a global computer network where anything from music to software can be copied and distributed at the click of a mouse, has ripped up the traditional copyright rulebooks.
At the conference, an army of bureaucrats are debating a stack of proposals covering literary and artistic works, the rights of performers and producers of music and of databases.
At stake are billions of dollars and the future of the electronic information industry, the up-and-coming medium for the distribution of music, literature, software and commerce.
Supporters say the pacts only extend existing intellectual property rights covered by the century-old Berne convention.

But attempts by copyright-based industries to ensure they get a cut from online works have led to a storm of protests by critics, who say the pacts will block the public's information to electronic information from stock prices to football results.
Telephone companies have joined in the fray, saying the draft treaties make them liable to electronic information carried on their lines.
"It comes down to money. Copyright industries want the money and they don't want another medium to grow. They're afraid of it," said Larry Clinton of the U.S. Telephone Association.
"We are having problems with the same people who opposed televisions and videos in their early days. There's always been this anti-technology bias," he added.

Network providers said they were hopeful the protests would prompt a rethink on the pacts which they say make even innocent Web-surfing, which by definition requires that a computer make transient copies, a violation of copyright rules.
"We're not interested in being the copyright cops. I'm optimistic we're going to make some progress," said Aubrey Sarvis of U.S. telephone company Bell Atlantic.
"Within the U.S. delegation, we've seen more flexibility and greater awareness among colleagues from other countries."
